findings.title: Device is cached before the limit check, so a rejected device is let in on its next request
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and it caches whether or not the call succeeds. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request is rejected in `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The device ID is now in the local cache, though, so every following request within the 29-minute TTL returns nil early from `tagDeviceUI` and authenticates. The limit therefore blocks only one request per device per cache period (per instance) and does not really enforce anything. The cache entry should be set only after a successful create/update, or the rejection should be cached and checked.

findings.title: Device limit is bypassed by omitting the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header
findings.body: `TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing. It also returns nil when the remote IP cannot be parsed. In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds without any limit check. The header is fully client-controlled, so any client that leaves it out (curl, scripts, or a modified frontend) gets anonymous access no matter how many devices are already registered. Only cooperating UI clients are affected by the limit. If the limit is meant as an access control, requests without a device ID need a defined policy, such as rejecting them once the limit is enabled and reached.

findings.title: Non-atomic count-then-insert lets the device limit be exceeded
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate statement with no transaction or lock, runs the upsert. Concurrent requests from new devices, within one instance or across HA replicas, can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The stored device count can end up well above the configured limit. The check and the insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with a count guard, or a transaction with appropriate locking.

findings.title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path for all deployments, adding a COUNT(*) per new device
findings.body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` with the request context for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. On each local-cache miss the request waits for a DB upsert. When a limit is set, it also waits for a `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN` over the whole anon_device table. The cache key is the client-supplied device ID, so a client sending random IDs forces these queries on every request and adds DB load and latency to anonymous auth. Consider keeping the async path when no limit is configured, and caching the device count instead of counting per request.

findings.title: ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64, which breaks wire injection of anonstore.AnonStore
findings.body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` through dependency injection, which implies `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is registered as a wire provider (in `pkg/server/wire.go`). The provider signature is now `ProvideAnonDBStore(db.DB, int64)`. Wire cannot resolve a bare `int64`, so code generation fails if the provider is still registered. Any other consumer that injects `anonstore.AnonStore` also loses its provider, or gets a separately constructed store without the limit. wire.go is not part of this change and needs updating, or the limit should come from `*setting.Cfg`.

findings.title: rowsAffected==0 is treated as limit reached, but MySQL reports 0 for unchanged rows
findings.body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. With the default go-sql-driver/mysql settings (no clientFoundRows), MySQL counts only rows whose values actually changed. `updated_at` is a second-precision DATETIME, so an update with the same IP, user agent and second (for example, the same device tagged by two HA instances, whose local caches are separate) reports 0 rows. An already-registered device is then rejected as over the limit.

findings.title: Limit test does not cover updating an existing device at the limit or the auth-level behavior
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not check the main intended behavior: an already-registered device must still be able to update when the limit is reached. No test covers `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejecting a device over the limit, or repeated requests from a rejected device. Such a test would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`.

findings.title: New `device_limit` setting not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documentation
findings.body: The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` key is read here, but `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the configuration docs are not updated. Operators have no way to discover the option, or to learn that 0 means unlimited and that devices over the limit lose anonymous access.

findings.title: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` infers type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig
findings.body: With strictNullChecks, a class field initialized to `undefined` without a type annotation gets the type `undefined`. Code using `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` (typed as `GrafanaBootConfig`) therefore cannot treat it as a number; for example, `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` is a type error. The backend always sends an int64 (0 by default), never undefined. The field should be annotated, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`, or simply default to 0.
